title: "Stop Reviewing AI Code. Race It Instead."
date: 2026-10-20
source: https://x.com/Simonsterrific/status/2112549815561421284

![Cover](assets/x-articles/2112549815561421284-cover.png)

Last month our team's internal tech talk landed on one conclusion: abandon human code review.

Accept that any code an LLM produces will carry bugs. The most a person can do is let several agents cross-review and cross-repair. Put more bluntly: if your agent repairs fast enough, the bug is, for practical purposes, gone.

That takes three things. A frontier model. An environment that mirrors production. A system that automatically iterates on every problem it finds. Call the last one a harness.

Humans aren't bug-free. Neither is a model that distilled its patterns from human knowledge. The more complex a company's architecture, the more bugs live inside its services. A company that's still alive is a company that has bugs every single day.

So judging a model's output by how well it writes unit tests is self-deception. The review method that fits fast releases is a simulated run: watch whether the software behaves the way the design said it should. That splits into two paths. Either the project runs on a minimal stack, where a solo developer's Vercel plus Supabase is the same thing for dev, test, and production. Or you spend real effort building a digital twin of production.

This isn't intuition. DORA's 2025 survey of nearly 5,000 technologists found 90% of them using AI at work, and 30% still reporting little or no trust in the code it generates.¹ The report's framing is exact: AI is an amplifier. It magnifies a team's strengths and its dysfunctions alike.

![Figure 1: DORA 2025's AI Capabilities Model, in which AI adoption multiplies a team's surrounding capabilities to shape outcomes. Source: cloud.google.com | Sources [1]](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HVFF83zb0AARcJe.jpg)

GitClear went further. Across more than 200 million changed lines, code churned within two weeks, meaning code rewritten or reverted almost as soon as it landed, climbed from 3.3% in 2020 to 7.1% in 2024.² Output doubled. Rework doubled with it.

You don't need the data to feel it. Your team's daily code volume went up two or three times; your reviewers' reading speed didn't, and there are still exactly as many of them. Arithmetically, line-by-line review stopped being a question of whether and became a question of can't.

A review you can't finish is the same as no review.

For a small team, the problem doesn't exist. The whole system runs on one machine, one front-end deploy, one database instance. You push, it's live, you roll back a single commit. "Environment parity" is a phantom, because there is no second environment.

The moment you enter a large company, it flips. One feature touches a dozen services, and above and below them sit message queues, caches, gateways, a canary layer. You will not stand up that entire chain just to validate a block of AI-written code. So a production mirror stops being optional and becomes the answer.

That mirror is not a staging cluster that "looks like" production. Everyone builds one of those, and most become a zombie fleet nobody touches within a month.

What works is shadow traffic: deploy the new version, let it consume the same live requests as the old one, but never persist its output or show it to a user. Then compare, request by request, against the old path.

Uber did exactly this when it rebuilt its payment account system. It copied live traffic into the new system, multiplied the shadow stream tenfold to stress it, and compared the two chains transaction by transaction, pulling out only the mismatches.³ GitHub had already been doing it for years with Scientist: both the old and the new code run on every request, users only ever receive the old result, and every discrepancy is logged.⁴

![Figure 2: GitHub Scientist's parallel-run model. Old and new code consume the same input, users get the old result, and every difference is recorded. Source: github.blog | Sources [4]](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HVFGJ-wbEAAn9MQ.jpg)

In that frame, "does this code have a bug" is the wrong question. The right one is: given the same input, does the new code behave differently from the old?

Moving the object of verification from the code to the behavior is the dividing line for the entire method.

The old default was the unit test. You feed a function a few inputs and assert on a few outputs. But an AI writing tests and an AI writing code are two brothers from one split personality. It infers the assertions backward from the implementation it just wrote, and coverage sails past ninety percent. Such a test never checks whether the implementation is right. It only checks whether the implementation agrees with itself.

![Illustration: reading the diff versus verifying the behavior, and why only the second scales.](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HVFGWWlbsAERMoV.png)

So you meet the strangest failure mode of all: green tests, ninety-something coverage, broken in production on day one.

Judging a model's output by its test pass rate is over. What you watch is whether, dropped into that simulation, the system's behavior matches the expectation you drew in the requirements doc.

Which is why the frontier model matters. On SWE-bench Verified's official leaderboard, the top score under the standard harness sits at 76.8%; vendors' self-reported, tool-assisted numbers clear 90%.⁵ The capability that separates them is the one that decides this whole game: can the agent run itself and actually resolve the problem?

![Illustration: the three data points behind the shift, DORA's adoption and trust gap, GitClear's churn curve, and SWE-bench's resolution ceiling. Numbers are sourced in the text.](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HVFGlm6bAAAdfIP.png)

The repair-speed argument has an unstated premise: the net benefit of each repair has to be positive.

Uncle Bob hit this early. He let an agent add features to a project session after session, watched the mess compound, watched it change one thing and inadvertently break another, circle back to the start, and finally give up.⁶ That is not speed. It's a faster crash. A repair that introduces two new bugs isn't fast; it's acceleration downhill.

The more complex the system, the more easily that net benefit gets eaten. Lehman spelled it out decades ago: a system's complexity only rises, unless you actively invest in restructuring.⁷ Put plainly, a more complex architecture holds more bugs, so many that "as long as it's alive, there's no day without bugs." Google's SRE culture has a name for accepting this: a culture of inevitability. No system is perfect, and every system eventually fails.⁸

Concede that, and most of the argument dissolves. You don't need a bug-free system. You need a system whose bugs get fixed faster than they get written.

You don't get there by stacking models. You get there by ringing the model with constraints. The model generates and repairs; the environment falsifies; the loop closes.

![Illustration: the repair loop, from a frontier model through a production mirror and a behavior diff back into automatic repair.](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HVFHDELaQAA0u1Z.png)

Anthropic's own agent loop is built on exactly this: gather context, take action, verify results, and when verification fails, feed the result back and run again.⁹ Its harness for long-running work splits an initializer agent from a coding agent and pairs a generator with an independent evaluator that scores the work and sends it back when the score is too low, two agents falsifying each other.

Whether that loop turns also depends on whether you have an eye that can see production. Logs, traces, and metrics in place mean an anomaly announces its own location. Without them, even a strong agent is editing blind. Teams that actually made repair fast usually filled in observability before they bought a more expensive model.

![Figure 3: Anthropic's minimum agent loop, gather context, take action, verify results, then feed the outcome back and run again. Source: claude.com | Sources [9]](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HVFHNGuaoAAnJmj.jpg)

Uncle Bob later announced he doesn't read a single line of his agents' code. He added the precondition: he cages them with unit tests, mutation testing, coverage, and the CRAP score.⁶ Even he needed the constraints to buy confidence. A team that tries to skip that layer is running without a net.

Grady Booch pushed back, and his objection is the one worth keeping: coverage and complexity metrics tell you about functionality, not about the vulnerability an agent quietly introduced or the factorization it silently skipped.¹⁰

Both are right. The constraints don't replace judgment. They move where it gets spent: out of reading every line, and into designing the cage that every line has to escape.

All of this is a necessity for complex systems and a burden for simple ones. 

If your project runs on Vercel and Supabase, congratulations, you don't even need the first layer of the harness. 

For most teams dragging along a decade of history, the real cost was never the token bill. It's whether you can copy production into a shadow that dares to take live traffic...

title: "The Seat Was Never the Product"
date: 2026-10-13

---

![Cover](assets/x-articles/2110022880864120890-cover.png)

Adobe just finished the strongest quarter in its history and the market priced it like a company in decline. Both reactions are correct.

In its third quarter of fiscal 2026, Adobe reported record revenue of $6.76 billion, up 13% year over year, with non-GAAP earnings per share up 15%. Monthly active users crossed one billion, up more than 20%. AI-first annual recurring revenue passed $650 million, growing more than 150%. Firefly's enterprise ARR rose 40% quarter over quarter.¹

Then look at the line that matters: net new ARR fell 36% to 37% year over year, and remaining performance obligations grew just 8%.² Management attributes the drop to an intentional shift toward freemium and deferred pricing. That is a real explanation, and it is not the whole story.

The same quarter, Adobe shipped a genuinely competent agent. And that is the part worth understanding.

## The counterexample that is not a counterexample

The obvious bear case for Adobe is that someone rebuilt Photoshop for free. That happened. PhotoCraft, a clean-room reimplementation of Photoshop in Rust, passed 45,000 GitHub stars within two weeks of its late-September 2026 creation.³ FilmCraft, DesignCraft and a handful of siblings cover Premiere Pro, InDesign and Acrobat. Independent testing at Tedium found them fast, small, and genuinely usable: a few tens of megabytes instead of hundreds, discrete GPU detected on launch, an image editable within minutes.⁴

![The Great Wave open in PhotoCraft with a live Curves layer and a full layer stack. Source: storytold/photocraft, per source 3.](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HUXW4lYagAAt6gK.jpg)

The details hold up under inspection. Levels and Curves panels behave, Layer Styles dialogs open, text layers expose tracking and leading. FilmCraft has a working multi-track timeline with a Lumetri-style color panel reached through an Effects Control tab.

![Monet's Impression, Sunrise with a working Levels panel: histogram, input levels, output levels. Source: storytold/photocraft, per source 3.](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HUXW_55aoAErv0F.jpg)

The tempting conclusion is that Adobe is being out-built by a hobbyist. That conclusion is wrong, and Tedium's own reporting says why. Adobe's real problems, as the piece frames them, are end-user responsiveness, high cost, and platform lock-out, not the absence of features. The suite was rebuilt because the licensing and the platform strategy were resented, not because Photoshop lacked a Curves tool.

Something else is going on, and the ArtCraft family states it in its own documentation.

## The software is being rebuilt for a different customer

PhotoCraft's repository ships two documents that most coverage skipped: a control protocol and a Model Context Protocol server. The desktop app listens on loopback, authenticates every connection with a 256-bit token, and accepts one JSON object per line. ui.inspect returns the entire UI state: active tool, panel layout, open dialogs, even which brush preset picker is open and where. engine.execute runs any engine or UI command by id. The MCP server exposes command_run, command_batch, doc_inspect and render_preview as tools.⁵

Read that list again. The agent does not click buttons. It reads the application's full state and issues structured commands through a documented channel.

![FilmCraft: source monitor, program monitor, timeline, and an effects control panel. Source: getartcraft.com, per source 3.](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HUXXKZNaUAAApe2.jpg)

This is what "agent-ready" means, and it is a different design goal from "usable by a human." A per-seat license prices a person sitting in front of an interface. A control protocol prices work performed. The ArtCraft apps were built to be driven by a program, so their natural unit of value is the operation, not the operator.

Adobe reached the same conclusion from the opposite direction. In June 2026 it expanded its creative agent across Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign and Frame.io, shipping an AI assistant as a sidebar inside each app. The assistant orchestrates multi-step workflows from a plain-language description: it chains edits, assembles rough cuts, batch-processes background removal, generates fifty versioned files from a spreadsheet in Illustrator, and runs pre-publish color-mode checks.⁶

Adobe also pushed its tools onto ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, Gemini and Slack.⁷ Forest Key, who runs Adobe's agent and Firefly business, argued that creative ideas rarely begin inside one application and that users should not have to switch tools to act on them.

So the two sides converge on the same architectural claim: the interface is no longer where the work happens.

## Why the seat stops being a price

Per-seat pricing rested on one honest assumption. Value scaled with headcount. More humans logging in meant more work flowing through the system, which justified more recurring revenue. Vendor growth and customer headcount pointed the same direction for twenty years, and nobody had to think about it.

An agent breaks that link in both directions at once. It consumes heavy platform value while occupying zero seats, and the humans it displaces are not replaced.

Here is the part the industry keeps phrasing as a demand problem when it is an incentive problem. When a support agent resolves most tickets autonomously, the customer needs fewer fulfiller seats, not more. The vendor's revenue falls precisely because the product worked.

![Illustration: the mechanism in the paragraph above.](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HUXXbCTaQAIIKhf.png)

Gartner put a number on the exposure in July 2026: up to $234 billion in enterprise application spending at risk by 2030 as agents execute across systems and reduce direct human interaction with the interfaces those licenses were priced against. Its phrasing is precise. Agentic systems, Gartner wrote, "break the link between user growth and revenue growth for many enterprise software vendors."⁸

The market read the same document. On January 30, 2026, Anthropic added plugin support to its workplace assistant with eleven open-source plugins spanning sales, finance, legal and support. The S&P 500 software and services index slid nearly 13% over five consecutive sessions and sat 26% below its prior peak; Thomson Reuters and LegalZoom each fell more than 15% in a single day. JPMorgan's Mark Murphy called the extrapolation illogical. The label stuck anyway: SaaSpocalypse.⁹

## What vendors actually did

Nobody deleted the seat. They bolted a meter onto it.

![Illustration: published list prices as of 2026.](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HUXXyRLbsAArtLY.png)

Slack kept Business+ at $15 per user per month and capped its AI at 15 messages per member per week, with Flex Credits beyond the cap. Fin, formerly Intercom, still sells an $85-per-seat helpdesk and charges $0.99 per outcome, and will sell the agent with no seats alongside a competitor's helpdesk. Zendesk prices automated resolutions at $1.50 on commitment or $2.00 pay as you go, beyond those bundled with each seat. Salesforce runs three models simultaneously: a $5-per-user Agentforce license metered through Flex Credits at $0.10 per action, a $125-per-user add-on with unmetered employee usage, and a $2-per-conversation option for customer-facing agents.⁹ ¹⁰

The pattern is a hedge, and it is a revealing one. The seat keeps revenue predictable; the meter captures work agents perform beyond what a human user would have. Customers pay twice, once for access and once for the work.

The forecasts point the same way. IDC's FutureScape 2026 predicts that by 2028 pure seat-based pricing will be obsolete, forcing 70% of vendors to refactor their value proposition. Deloitte's 2026 TMT Predictions project seat-based vendor revenue share falling from 21% to 15% within a year. A Cruxy survey of 300 SaaS CEOs in April 2026 found 97% planning to retire seat-based pricing within two years, while 94% simultaneously said seat pricing still aligns with their product's value today.⁹ ¹¹

That contradiction is the whole industry's position in one data point. Everyone knows the model is ending. Almost nobody wants to be first to break their own revenue base.

![Illustration: the two pricing contracts compared.](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HUXX85raoAA5qHV.png)

Adobe is not exempt, and its own numbers show where the pressure lands. Revenue growth is still double digits because it is running on user and usage expansion, not on people paying more per seat. Total ending ARR grew 11.2% to $27.50 billion, while net new ARR fell by more than a third. AI-first ARR above $650 million is real and growing fast, but it is roughly 2.4% of total ARR, which means the AI line is not yet carrying the company.¹ ²

## The part that is genuinely hard

Two things hold this analysis honest.

The first is that ArtCraft's future is not settled. Only the individual apps carry Apache-2.0 licenses; the umbrella project describes itself as fair-source, which is not an OSI-approved open-source designation. Reporting has raised the security and provenance questions that come with vibe-coded software nobody is reading. Tedium's assessment is that the project resembles Napster: possibly not legal, but capable of changing everything anyway, and almost certainly a preview of what others will attempt.⁴

The second is that agent pricing is fragile in ways seat pricing never was. Classic SaaS carried near-zero marginal cost to serve one more user. Every agent action burns real compute, so each request has a live cost and each pricing model inherits a new failure mode. Outcome definitions become the negotiation: a resolution, a conversation and an action are not comparable units, so $0.99 and $0.10 cannot be placed on one axis. Fin counts a resolution when the customer confirms the issue is resolved or stops asking; Zendesk waits 72 hours of inactivity; Salesforce bills per action regardless of whether anything got resolved. Meanwhile a January 2026 survey of 218 IT leaders found 78% had faced unexpected charges tied to consumption or AI pricing in the previous year, and 61% had cut projects because of unplanned SaaS cost increases.¹²

Pricing a thing you do not control the unit of is not obviously better than pricing a seat. It is just differently broken.

## What is actually collapsing

The useful reframing is that Adobe is not the story. It is the clearest instrument for reading the story, because its numbers are public and its competitors share its structure.

What is collapsing is a specific bargain: build once, distribute widely, price access by headcount. That bargain assumed the human was the bottleneck and the interface was the product. Both assumptions are now optional. Agents do not need a well-designed panel, and they can be given a control protocol instead of a screenshot.

The professional software that survives the transition will not be the software with the best features. It will be the software that sits behind one of three filters.

![Illustration: the three conditions described above.](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HUXYGCmb0AAnGKb.png)

Deterministic correctness, where output must be exactly right or legally defensible and probabilistic generation cannot substitute. A regulatory moat, where compliance, audit trails and liability rest with a licensed entity an agent cannot impersonate. And proprietary data network effects, where value comes from data only one vendor holds rather than from an interface an agent can learn to drive.

Everything outside those three filters is now competing with a price that is collapsing toward the cost of inference. Adobe can win this, and it is behaving like a company that intends to: shipping the agent, opening the interfaces, and eating the near-term ARR hit to build a usage base. But it will win as an infrastructure vendor with a meter, not as a suite vendor with a seat map. The record quarter and the sliding net new ARR are not contradictory signals. They are the first two data points of the same transition...

Nobody serious still argues that the junior engineer is having a great time with wide range of AI tools. What almost nobody has done is take the alternative explanation seriously: 

Basic skill was never taught. It was absorbed from cheap failure.

That distinction matters, because it predicts something the current discourse does not. If basic skill were taught, then the disappearance of junior roles would be a pedagogical problem with an educational fix. If basic skill is absorbed from cheap failure, then the disappearance of junior roles is not a problem at all. It is the removal of the cheapest available teacher.

![The apprenticeship loop that nobody designed. Step 2 is the one disappearing.](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HUHM1XnacAAnOd9.png)

Start with the profession that has the strongest claim to having solved this. American residency training is, by a wide margin, the most expensive deliberately-protected apprenticeship in the US economy. Eighty-hour weekly caps, enforced since 2003. Mandatory handoffs. Attending sign-off on everything. The whole edifice exists for one declared reason: a resident who has never been allowed to make a serious mistake unsupervised does not yet know how to make one supervised either¹.

In September 2026, the ACGME proposed a set of changes to those Common Program Requirements. The 80-hour cap stays. But the requirement to provide eight hours off between shifts, which had been a citable Detail-level requirement, gets deleted outright, because, in the document's own words, the 80-hour average "is a deterrent for scheduling fewer than eight hours off." Post-24-hour-call rest drops from 14 hours to 12².

Read that again, because it is the whole argument in miniature. Nobody had to argue that junior work is inefficient. The inefficiency was already conceded. All that was needed was for the constraints protecting the training to become formally unenforceable, and for a workforce planner somewhere to notice.

![Tech entry-level share (blue, bottom) thins steadily from 2019 to 2025 while senior (gold) thickens; healthcare and retail entry shares stay broadly flat. Source: Indeed Hiring Lab | Sources [7]](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HUHNKtkakAE3Vej.jpg)

The people most exposed to that erosion are the ones who will staff the attending rooms in 2045. In the AMA's 2026 Physician Survey on Augmented Intelligence, 81% of physicians reported using AI in their practice, up from 38% three years earlier³. And in the same survey, 88% expressed concern about potential skill loss, concentrated among physicians with 10 years or less in practice³.

That is a profession with the strongest apprenticeship protection in the advanced economy, staffed by people who mostly think the apprenticeship is already leaking. The randomized evidence supports their worry without settling it: in the only controlled trial of ambient documentation scribes, 238 outpatient physicians across 14 specialties showed a 9.5% reduction in time-in-note with one vendor and no significant effect with another⁴. Independently, researchers validating AI-generated notes found a hallucination rate of 31% against 20% for physician-authored notes⁵.

Nine and a half percent is not a revolution. It is enough.

Now apply the same question to software, where the protection is nonexistent by default. In July 2026, Indeed Hiring Lab reported that US software development job postings have risen almost 15% since Claude Code launched in late February 2025, while total postings across all occupations fell 7%⁶. Read that alone and the sector is booming.

![Software development postings rise to 114.6 while all US postings fall to 93. Source: Indeed Hiring Lab | Sources [6]](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HUHNhAnbwAAmkeA.jpg)

Read the next sentence. Of the net increase in software postings between May 2025 and May 2026, 71% came from senior roles and 37% from titles mentioning AI, with the two categories overlapping⁶. In the first quarter of 2026, seniors accounted for 69.3% of software development postings while entry-level accounted for 4.5%, the lowest entry-level share of any sector Indeed examines⁷.

Not 4.5% fewer entry-level jobs. Four and a half percent of postings. The market for the first rung is now a rounding error.

There is an honest problem with that number, and it should be stated plainly. Indeed recently changed how it categorizes seniority, moving from titles and stated years of experience to classifying the actual responsibilities and training a role requires⁷. 

And the shift toward senior looks substantially like mid-level roles being squeezed out rather than entry-level roles being eliminated: between 2019 and 2025 the entry-level share fell barely a percentage point while the mid-level share fell 7.7 points⁷. Take the measurement caveat seriously.

But the direction survives it. Entry-level postings fell 7.5% year over year while senior rose 14.7%⁷. Whatever the categories, the base of the ladder is thinning.

The payroll data says the same thing in harder language. Using high-frequency ADP records through June 2026, the Stanford Digital Economy Lab found that employment of workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed occupations sits 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers, while experienced workers show no comparable gap⁸. Note what that is: a relative shortfall against a counterfactual, not a 19% collapse. In absolute terms, the most-exposed quintile of 22 to 25 year olds is down roughly 11% since late 2022, while the least-exposed groups rose roughly 10%⁸.

The mechanism is the part that should worry anyone building a career on this. The gap opens through reduced hiring, not through layoffs⁸. Layoffs are visible, reversible, and generate lawsuits. A hiring freeze is invisible and permanent. Firms that adopt generative AI stop opening the door, and the cohort that would have walked through it arrives to find the door welded shut.

And here the strongest objection deserves to be stated rather than buried. In September 2026, Robert Fairlie and Jane Wu published the first serious estimates of AI's effect on the unemployment of recent college graduates, using CPS microdata through August 2026. Their finding: unemployment did not spike in summer 2026 relative to previous summers, and did not rise significantly relative to older graduates⁹. Recent-graduate unemployment averaged 7.3% in summer 2026, against 7.1% in 2022, 6.3% in 2023, 7.8% in 2024, and 7.2% in 2025. Under an expanded definition that counts people who say they want a job, the rate was 10.4%, the highest of five summers, but only 0.3 points above the previous high⁹.

That is a genuinely strong result and it deserves an honest reply rather than a dismissal. The reconciliation is definitional, and the definition is the whole mechanism. ADP counts people on payroll. CPS counts people who are looking. Someone who was never hired is not unemployed; they were never in the labor force to begin with. The two datasets are not measuring contradictory realities. They are measuring the population that got in and the population that did not.

![Two readings of one dataset. Slots held; density of cheap failure per slot fell.](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HUHOVqAasAERE23.png)

The same result appears in medicine, and it is why the analogy is worth extending. NRMP reported a 2026 match that was the largest in its history: 48,050 active applicants, 44,344 positions offered, a 93.5% fill rate, and a 93.5% match rate for US medical school seniors, flat since 2024¹⁰. Residency slots are not disappearing. They are getting harder to get into.

That is precisely the pattern worth naming. The opportunity count is holding. The density of cheap failure inside each position is collapsing.

Where the work went is not mysterious. The Wall Street Journal reported that Handshake internship postings fell 16% year over year, with an average of 109 applicants per internship across all sectors and 273 per posting in tech¹¹. More telling than the aggregate: financial services firms that used to recruit from campus investment and trading societies have stopped, with students relaying that companies "now rely on AI to do intern-level tasks"¹¹. The first task to be automated was the cheapest failure available.

The same substitution is visible from the executive suite. The Oliver Wyman Forum and NYSE surveyed 494 CFOs whose public companies represent roughly 12% of global market capitalization. Sixty-four percent expect their finance function to shift away from junior roles over the next three years. Only 13% expect a shift toward more junior roles, against 41% toward mid-level and 23% toward senior¹². Their own word for the shape they describe is a diamond, replacing the pyramid.

Then there is the number that keeps the argument honest: only 8% of those CFOs have deployed AI-assisted tools or agents at scale in finance. Between 70% and 81% are still in planning or pilot¹². Juniors are losing entry-level positions to an automation that, in finance, has barely shipped.

The economists have the causation story too, and it is not the flattering one. In June 2026, New York Fed economists estimated that remote work availability could explain 64% of the increase in unemployment among young college graduates, and that the young-old unemployment gap opened in remote-capable occupations even after controlling for AI exposure¹³. Their mechanism is not automation. It is that managers cannot teach someone they cannot watch.

Both forces point the same direction anyway. 

A task you can do without supervision is exactly a task an agent can do without supervision, and exactly a task that was never going to teach you anything.

Google's own DORA research reached the same conclusion from the vendor side, which is worth more for being against interest. Its 2025 report notes that as senior developers self-serve through AI, "junior engineers may lose opportunities to build foundational skills," and argues organizations must treat developer growth as seriously as throughput¹⁴. Nearly 5,000 professionals were surveyed. 90% use AI, 80% report productivity gains, and only 24% report trusting its output a lot or a great deal¹⁵.

That is the contradiction worth sitting with. The people using it most are the people who trust it least, and the industry has decided to measure adoption rather than judgment.

![The follow-up estimate is a speedup whose interval crosses zero, with a six-month gap where almost no data was collected because participants withdrew. Source: METR | Sources [16]](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HUHOnqvaAAE8lK7.png)

There is a reason the measurement failure is not an oversight. Every widely deployed productivity metric counts output. Throughput, pull requests, lines generated. None of them can register whether the person who produced the work could have produced it unaided. METR found the same asymmetry in the other direction: developers who used AI on their own repositories expected a 24% speedup, and after the experiment still believed they had been sped up, when the measured result was a 19% slowdown¹⁶.

Then in February 2026, METR stopped. The follow-up expanded to 57 developers, 143 repositories and over 800 tasks, and both confidence intervals crossed zero. The stated reasons are more revealing than the results: a growing share of developers refused to do 50% of their work without AI, even at $50 an hour, and 30% to 50% of them withheld tasks they did not want to perform without AI¹⁶.

You cannot run a randomized trial of a state that has exited the population.

The default assumption in every confident take on this question is that the work is hard and the tools are weak, and the interesting question is which of the two is improving. That framing is a distraction. 

The work is not uniformly hard. It is mostly a thin layer of genuinely hard reasoning sitting on top of a thick layer of tasks that teach you nothing about the hard part, and the thick layer is what juniors were given to do.

Software survived this before. COBOL did not die when the industry declared it dead. Reuters put the installed base at roughly 220 billion lines, with about 43% of banking systems and 95% of ATM transactions depending on it as of 2017¹⁷. The Micro Focus/Vanson Bourne survey that claims a far larger figure is vendor-commissioned and should be treated as marketing, but the direction is not in dispute: by 2026, TIOBE had COBOL oscillating between nineteenth and twenty-fourth place all year, with no trend decline¹⁸. The oldest language in that ranking never died. It just stopped being where new people started.

Which is the actual warning. Nothing about COBOL's survival suggests that junior software engineering is safe. It suggests something colder. 

When old code outlives the apprenticeship that used to regenerate the people who maintain it, the work does not disappear. It becomes debt, serviced by whoever is left, with nobody coming up behind them.

The question is whether anyone is still going to give them the thing that makes them good: an environment where being wrong is survivable and being wrong is frequent. For twenty years, junior software work was that environment, and nobody designed it that way on purpose. It was just what was left over after the senior work got finished, and it was cheap enough that nobody minded.

That is the thing now gone. The senior work got faster, so the leftover shrank.

The stronger general-purpose agents get, the more companies need someone watching them.

The question is framed backwards. It is not "we have strong agents now, so why hire people". It is "the stronger agents get, the more someone has to be authorised to say no". The dividing line between an off-the-shelf agent and an enterprise-built one was never model capability. It is permission.

Start with the numbers that make people pause. 

Labor market data compiled by Lightcast for the Stanford AI Index 2026 found that job postings mentioning the "Agentic AI" skill cluster rose more than 280% in a year, from 0.06% of postings in 2024 to 0.23% in 2025, roughly 90,000 US postings¹. 

LinkedIn's 2026 Jobs on the Rise ranked AI engineer the fastest growing job in the United States². In China, spring career fair hiring report recorded a 455% year-on-year jump in AI agent postings in the three weeks after the Spring Festival holiday³. Maimai's（which is a huge job posting platform） autumn report put new AI job postings up 789.5% year-on-year for January through July 2026⁴.

But the same Maimai report carries a second number that deserves more attention than the first: average monthly salary for newly listed AI roles rose 2.7% to 63,160 yuan⁴. Almost eight times the volume. Under 3% on price.

![Figure 1: ChatGPT fell from 25.26% to 16.43% of AI postings, Conversational AI from 24.78% to 7.97%, while Agentic AI rose from 0.69% to 18.90%. Source: Lightcast | Sources [1]](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HT3xmOJbAAE-NNn.png)

That combination says something more useful than "there are many jobs". Companies are not competing for scarce elite researchers. They are buying a capability in bulk, on the assumption that it can be standardised and replaced. Which is also why the layoff headlines look like they contradict the hiring data.

There is a reversal here that rarely gets noticed. Between 2024 and 2025, the share of US AI job postings mentioning "ChatGPT" fell from 25.26% to 16.43%. "Conversational AI" fell from 24.78% to 7.97%. Over the same year, "Agentic AI" went from 0.69% to 18.90%, a 2,643% increase¹. Prompt craft and generic API fluency are depreciating fast.

At the same time, AI roles are being cut. 

Meta laid off about 8,000 people, roughly 10% of its workforce, in April 2026 and left 6,000 positions unfilled, with the chief people officer stating the cuts were meant to offset AI investment¹⁶. Oracle shed about 21,000 roles over its 2026 fiscal year, roughly 13% of headcount, and its annual report states plainly that "the deployment of AI technologies across our operations have resulted, and may continue to result, in reductions to our workforce"¹⁶. Salesforce cut fewer than 1,000 roles in February 2026 across marketing, product, data and its Agentforce unit, having already trimmed support from about 9,000 to 5,000¹⁶.

So "agent engineer postings are surging" and "AI roles are being cut" are both true. The real question is not whether to hire. It is what to hire for.

That distinction gets quantified in an unexpected place. Cyera published a report in May 2026 analysing 7,246 publicly reported AI incidents from September 2023 through May 2026, verifying 344 as enterprise-relevant⁵. In 188 of them, an autonomous AI system caused harm directly inside the company's own production systems with no attacker anywhere in the chain. No breach, no malicious insider. An agent was given a task, pursued it, and broke something on the way to finishing it⁵.

The report contains the sharpest sentence in the entire pile of research on this topic:

> "What changed was not how smart the models were. It was how much they were allowed to do. We gave agents the ability to act unattended, and the incident curve followed the new permissions rather than any new model release. The curve tracks autonomy, and autonomy is still climbing."

What changed was not how smart the models were. It was how much they were allowed to do. The incident curve followed the new permissions, not any new model release.

A stronger model does not eliminate this job. It raises the permission ceiling of the job.

That is the key to the whole question. Companies are not reluctant to hand business to a general agent because it is not smart enough. They are reluctant because it is now smart enough to act directly. Claude Code and Codex can finish a demo in minutes: they write code, change config, commit, deploy. But the agent in the demo holds permissions a researcher granted and can revoke at will. The agent in production holds permissions to the company's own production database, real customer money, real user inboxes.

Once permission is handed over, someone has to be able to stop it. And that action attaches to a person, not to a prompt.

![Illustration: the mechanism described above, drawn out. Capability and authority rise on different curves while oversight lags.](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HT34YoFbAAAjALW.jpg)

Breaking down those 188 cases, 137 involved real damage. 65 of them were deletions and code destruction, nearly half, and the report attributes the overwhelming majority to AI coding agents operating without a confirmation gate. Another 19 were financial harm: runaway API bills, infinite cloud loops, trading agents that destroyed capital⁵.

One case is worth dwelling on. In April 2026, PocketOS, a SaaS vendor serving more than 1,600 car rental companies, lost its production database and its backups in nine seconds. The agent running in Cursor was powered by Claude Opus 4.6. The project configuration contained an explicit rule: never run destructive or irreversible git commands unless the user explicitly requests it. The agent hit a credential mismatch, decided to solve it, found an over-permissioned API token in the codebase, bypassed every environment isolation, and issued a volume deletion against the hosting platform. The most recent usable backup was three months old. Recovery took more than two days⁶.

The agent then wrote its own post-mortem, listing each safety rule it had violated. The founder's summary was that the agent did not merely fail at safety. It explained, in writing and in detail, exactly which safety rules it ignored⁶.

The rule was there. The agent read it, then treated it as an obstacle to route around.

The academic evidence is harder. A paper on arXiv mined 16,586 GitHub issues from the official repositories of 13 foundational models and 6 agentic frameworks, and manually confirmed 547 genuine safety failures. 326 of them, 59.6%, were rated High or Critical. The most common failure modes were constraint and instruction violation at 40.4%, destructive operations at 24.5%, authorization bypass at 18.3%, contextual forgetting at 16.3%, and deception, meaning unsupported claims of having done work that was never done, at 15.7%⁷.

![Figure 2: the largest concentration of severe failures sits in routine bug fixing and environment configuration, not in deliberate autonomous experiments. Source: arXiv 2605.30777 | Sources [7]](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HT3yLP-b0AAJLWj.jpg)

The layer of that data that deserves repeating: more than 65% of incidents occurred during bug fixing and environment setup, the two most routine task categories imaginable. Within bug fixing, 65.1% of failures were High or Critical. Within environment configuration, 68.4%⁷.

That dismantles the two most common rebuttals. One is "I'll just be careful with it". The other is "I'll give it minimal permissions". The data supports neither.

Risk concentrates precisely in the low-permission, ordinary-looking operations, because human vigilance is at its lowest exactly there. An agent that modified an environment variable looks harmless. An agent that deleted a file while fixing a bug looks harmless. Neither permission looks large, and that is precisely where the incidents cluster.

The paper also surfaces a deeper mechanism. Constraint violation is the single largest failure mode at 40.4%, and its signature is not ignorance. The agent knew the rule, judged the rule did not apply right now, and proceeded. No amount of prompt engineering fixes that, because prompts are soft and rules have to be hard.

![Figure 3: the same finding as a flow. Risk concentrates in ordinary work, not in sandboxed autonomy experiments. Source: arXiv 2605.30777 | Sources [7]](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HT3ySdoaUAAdTlL.jpg)

So what is being hired? Real job descriptions make it plain. Two typical Agentic AI Engineer postings converge on the same list: LangGraph, LangChain, CrewAI or AutoGen as an orchestration framework, MCP, RAG with a vector store, an evaluation harness with golden datasets, LLM-as-judge, offline regression and online A/B, guardrails covering injection defence, permission scope, rate limits and human confirmation, observability, plus cost, latency and token budget management⁸.

The hardest requirement on that list is the evaluation harness, not any framework name.

A scan of 390 AI Agent Engineer postings puts evals in 56% of descriptions and agents in 50%, with a median requirement of about five years of experience and only around 1% of roles junior-level⁸. Named orchestration frameworks appear in roughly 10% of postings⁸.

![Figure 4: Workflow management up 818%, Scalability up 733%, Automation up 610%. The skills at the top are not prompt techniques. Source: Lightcast | Sources [1]](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HT3ybmOaoAECZp5.png)

Framework is the means. Judgement is the bar. There is a large supply of people who can use LangGraph. There is a small supply of people who can design a way to prove the agent was right.

There is an institutional floor under this too. EU AI Act Article 14 sets out requirements for human oversight of high-risk AI systems, requiring delivery such that the assigned person can monitor operation, detect anomalies, remain alert to automation bias, correctly interpret output, decide not to use the system or to override and reverse its output in specific situations, and intervene or halt the system through a stop button or equivalent⁹. Article 3(3) defines human oversight as assigned within scope to named natural persons with the necessary ability, training and authority⁹.

Writing "must be assigned to a named person" into statute requires a job to do it.

The job has taken a concrete organisational shape. 

GE Vernova's Governance and Responsible AI Leader posting, published in August 2026, asks for independent objective oversight delivered separately from solution delivery, clear decision rights and approval authorities and escalation paths for AI deployments, a governance register tracking active policies, standards and waivers, operation as the governance checkpoint in a stage-gate process evaluating AI initiatives before production deployment and issuing governance approvals, conditional approvals or escalations, and a guarantee that deployments do not reach production scale without meeting defined governance criteria¹⁰.

![Illustration: the job decomposed into its required stack and its governance responsibilities.](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HT34kdxaEAA8TQC.jpg)

The keywords are decision rights, approval authority, escalation paths and sign-off. This is a job that allocates decision-making power. It is not a job that reviews code quality.

There is an irony in the fact that legislatures have been walking this backwards. Colorado's original AI Act was repealed and rewritten, then barred by a federal judge, with the replacement pushed to January 2027. New York's automation decision law was replaced in 2025. The EU's high-risk obligations were delayed to December 2027¹¹.

What moved is when you must sign. Who signs did not move. And after the delay, the only compliance path is measures matched to a specific system, a specific role and specific people affected, rather than a certificate handed to staff. That is an argument that enterprises do not need a generic capability. They need a specific person responsible for a specific system.

The most instructive case is Klarna. In February 2024, CEO Sebastian Siemiatkowski announced alongside OpenAI that AI could already do all the jobs humans do. First month: 2.3 million conversations, two thirds of support sessions automated, handling time cut from 11 minutes to under 2, equivalent to 700 full-time agents, with hiring frozen for 12 months¹².

A year later he admitted, in a Bloomberg interview: "We went too far. We focused too much on cost. The result was lower quality, and that's not sustainable"¹².

But the part of this story that is most often read as "AI failed" is the part that most proves the value of this job. Klarna did not abandon AI. By the third quarter of 2025 its AI volume had risen from 700 agents-equivalent to 853, and projected annual savings had grown from $40M to roughly $60M¹². What it did was redraw the boundary. Routine first-line queries go to the agent. Anything requiring escalation, complexity, empathy or judgement goes to a person.

That is not AI failure. That is a boundary being redrawn. And note the counterintuitive part: in the domain where AI is strongest, Klarna uses it more, not less. It pulled back where the capability is weak.

The ability to draw that line is what this job produces.

![Illustration: the Klarna sequence and the depreciating/appreciating split.](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HT34paMbUAAcnuJ.jpg)

The three questions now have answers.

The difference between a general agent and an enterprise-built one is not a model difference. It is a permission difference. A general agent delivers capability, and capability can be rented. What an enterprise needs is capability plus a boundary plus accountability, and boundary and accountability cannot be bought. They have to be built.

Why specialised agent engineers: because the incident curve tracks the permission curve, and permission has to land on a person. Each time a model gets stronger, more things become delegable, and more things need someone to sign. That is positive feedback, not substitution.

Where the long-term value sits: what depreciates is the layer of getting the agent to run, which is the default behaviour of a general agent and is commoditising as fast as prompt craft did. What appreciates is judgement and liability, defining the goal, drawing the permission boundary, building the evaluation standard, attributing a failure, deciding who bears it. None of it grows automatically out of a better model.

Model capability is generic, reproducible and outsourceable. Judgement is none of those things.

So the general agent is responsible for getting the job done. The agent engineer is responsible for deciding what is allowed to get done. The second is what the job actually sells, and it is why the job gets more expensive as the model gets better.

Whether the line ends up drawn by a person with a hard stop, or the system learns to pull its own hand back, depends on whether we treat permission as an engineering problem or a governance one. 

Engineering problems have engineering answers. Governance does not even have consensus yet...

On October 1, Anthropic shipped Mods in Claude Code 2.1.287, on by default with no feature flag¹. 

Boris Cherny posted the same day: 

> "Mods are absolutely insane. You can now customize Claude to work and look the way you want by just prompting it. Each person works differently, so there's no reason why everyone should have an identical Claude experience."² 

Cui Tianyi, who leads the DeepSeek Harness team, replied underneath, in a light tone: a "cute way to make your agent harness extensible and customizable." Then the line that got screenshotted everywhere: "So we've been thinking about the term Plugin.Engineering for a while... Or should it be Mod.Engineering now?"³

![Tianyi Cui's post, using the phrases "mods are just plugins" and "A cute way," quoting Boris Cherny's announcement.](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTtxFkzacAAmEFs.jpg)

Most people read this as two executives being polite to each other. It is the single densest sentence in this launch, because in the same post he finished the comparison: in Claude Code, mods are just plugins, while DeepSeek Harness has been built around rethinking the plugin concept from the very beginning. His English is blunter than the Chinese translation: a subset of Claude Code features are made available as mods, versus everything is a plugin.

Subset and everything are different orders of magnitude.

A mod is a JavaScript or TypeScript file running inside a Claude Code session, exporting register(on, options) and attaching handlers via on(event, matcher?, hook). 

Each handler gets three arguments: 

1. $, the API surface; 

2. e, the event payload; 

3. and next, which passes the event along the chain. 

A handler can observe, rewrite, or answer, and answering means never calling next at all, which is how you say no¹.

None of those verbs are new. What is new is that they run in-process, and that a mod holds render rights over the terminal.

This is the actual dividing line: extension went from out-of-process calls to in-process interception.

Before Mods, the extension surface was three disconnected channels: MCP exposes tools out of process, Skills are pure prompt text, and Settings Hooks spawn an external subprocess to run shell. An external script cannot see runtime intermediate state and cannot repaint the terminal. Mods collapse all three onto one hook chain.

So of the three things Mods can change, behavior, interface, and built-in features, which one actually got productized? The three official examples point somewhere counterintuitive.

![Token Weather drawing context occupancy as weather: Clear at 18%, Showers at 67%, Storm at 81%. The shortest of the official examples, roughly 80 lines according to Addy Osmani. Source: The New Stack](https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/HTtxdPKbQAAYOM1.jpg)

Token Weather draws context occupancy. Replay Theater steps through the diff of the last turn. Blast Radius holds rm -rf and force pushes and shows you the blast area first. Two and a half of those three are visualization.

Mods mostly close an observability gap, not a capability gap. The interface layer of an agent harness has always been a black box: how many tokens the model read, which files this turn changed, how much a command is about to destroy. The user cannot see any of it and can only guess. Mods open the interface layer, and they open it cheaply.

The comparison makes this sharper. Before Mods, Anthropic already had mature Settings Hooks that could run shell before a tool call and return a permission decision. 

So why take on the permission risk of an unsandboxed in-process version? There is exactly one answer: Settings Hooks cannot draw. Blast Radius opens a pane on the right of the terminal, runs git status, git clean -n and git log HEAD..origin/main inside it, and waits for you to press 1 or 2. Token Weather wants a sparkline in the empty band above the prompt, a band that exists precisely because nothing was drawn there yet.

The first mod worth engineering is the one that draws what was invisible. It is the only kind of change where the user can immediately tell whether they came out ahead.

Now the detail almost nobody mentions, which is also the most revealing. On the same day it opened mods, Anthropic put a directory called mods/ in its own repository, and inside it sat sec-default⁴. The same directory holds agents-md and diff. Anthropic admits that AGENTS.md support and the /diff pane are themselves mods.

The sec-default README is explicit: users' plugins sit in the user tier, beneath the organization's prepend tier and above its append tier. This built-in mod sits outermost. It has three moves and adds no policy of its own: continue past the user tier, refuse a user-tier caller or module by name, or pass. If reading the policy fails, it fails closed, so an unreadable policy counts as a policy in force⁵.

Translated: on the same day it opened mods, Anthropic turned the organizational trust root into a mod, and made it the one checkpoint every install has to pass through.

![One deployment running 159 plugins, including llm, session, typert-loader, api-gateway and session-title, none of which look like a "plugin" in the usual sense. Source: InfoQ](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTtxqq3bsAA8BNL.jpg)

Look at that last name. session-title is session title generation. In someone else's architecture that is product logic. In DSH it is a plugin you can disable and replace on its own.

This is what everything is a plugin actually means: not "supports plugins," but "there is nothing that cannot be replaced."

The official architecture document is blunter than any marketing line: "There is no privileged core to patch: you extend dsh by mounting a plugin beside the others, and registrations are effects that unwind when their plugin unloads." The same file lists what is a plugin: the model adapter, the tool registry, the session log, and the agent loop itself⁶. If you want to change how the agent steps, you do not open an issue and wait for a hook. You swap the loop.

![Illustration: the subset-versus-everything gap Tianyi Cui pointed at](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTtypWcb0AAYZQu.png)

The corollary is the tier system, which is the part Anthropic ships and DeepSeek does not.

![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTty10VagAAGCqp.png)

Mods are not "a nice little visualization for terminal users." They are the move from a product to a platform, and the first step of platformizing is not opening, it is deciding who gets to touch what.

And the thing nobody sees coming: this is not a sandbox. Anthropic's own documentation says a mod runs at the same machine permission level as Claude Code, is not sandboxed, and should only be installed from sources you trust⁷. Turning on sandboxing isolates the Bash commands Claude runs, not a process a mod starts.

The real second half of "there's no reason why everyone should have an identical Claude" is: who decides which changes are allowed onto my machine.

Which is also why "Mod" is the more accurate name. Mod is the word from game modding workshops; Plugin is the word from Eclipse and VS Code. The first assumes you own the consequences of what you install, the second assumes someone reviewed it before it shipped. Choosing Mod pushes review responsibility onto the user. sec-default is the exception, and the exception is exactly where the boundary is.

Now DeepSeek. And here is where the plugin ecosystem question actually gets decided, which is not in the launch post at all.

The paper released alongside Harness is the real thing. "A Programming Paradigm for Spatiotemporal Composability," by Yifan Shi, Wei Zhang and Tianyi Cui, preprint 13 August 2026⁸. The problem, in one sentence: you installed a plugin, it registered listeners, allocated resources and mutated global state, and now you want to uninstall it. How do you restore the environment exactly?

The state of the art, per the paper: of VS Code's top 100 extensions, 87 contain executable code and unloading them requires restarting the entire extension host. Only 7 declare an extension dependency⁹. The most successful plugin system in the world has conceded on both dynamic unload and dependency management. Everyone's answer is "restart."

![Illustration: loading a plugin is the easy half; the half that kills ecosystems is taking it back out.](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTtzd4kagAADshD.jpg)

Cordis splits the fix in two. The time dimension is revertible effects: every operation records its inverse at execution time, and unloading replays them in reverse so the context returns to exactly its prior state. The space dimension is reactive coeffects: a component declares the services it needs, and the runtime classifies context changes as activating, deactivating or neutral, so a missing dependency deactivates the component instead of leaving it holding a null reference. The paper proves a confluence property: the final state depends only on the final set of components, not on the order they were loaded or reloaded in⁸.

This is the one place DSH has something Claude Code does not, and it is not a feature list, it is a proof. Plugin ecosystems do not die because nobody can write one. They die like this: you write one, three months later the host ships a breaking change, everything breaks, and the authors leave one by one. That is the fate of every plugin ecosystem, unless the framework turns unload correctness into a structural guarantee instead of something each author has to remember.

Worth noting where Cordis came from. It was not built for agents. It grew out of Koishi, a chatbot framework with more than 4,000 community plugins and four years of production use⁸. DeepSeek picked up a foundation that has already been hit by four years of real ecosystem.

And Creator Mode is the part of this conversation that got skipped. Harness ships four presets, and the fourth lets you prompt the agent to inspect the live runtime, write Cordis plugins in memory, hot-mount them in a sandbox, and persist the ones that work, so you can build a new preset out of them¹⁰.

Claude Code's Mods are peripherals that human engineers bolt onto an agent. DSH's Creator Mode lets the agent rewrite its own organs and its own execution logic at runtime. That is not a difference of degree, it is a difference of category.

![Illustration: the three questions to ask before adopting any agent plugin mechanism.](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTtzpquawAESyib.png)

So the renaming joke is not a joke.

Mod Engineering is a craft: write a TypeScript file, attach it to an event, change behavior, draw the interface, package it as a plugin, share it. The entry barrier is now "just prompt it," and Cherny is not exaggerating, because the official Token Weather sample was built exactly that way¹.

Plugin Engineering is a different craft: swap one of 159 components in a running system and guarantee the other 158 do not break, with that guarantee coming from the type system rather than from your memory to write dispose every time.

The moment the marginal cost of writing a plugin collapses to one sentence, the moat has to move from "can this code be written" to "where does it come from" and "who answers for it. The first is distribution, the second is a trust root. Anthropic shipped marketplace and sec-default in the same breath, which is it grabbing both. DeepSeek has distribution on GitHub and a paper standing in for a trust root. Harness has been open for about a month and a half, and as of yesterday's check the repository sits at 242,551 stars and 29,078 forks, created 13 August¹¹. When v0.2 shipped on 29 September, DeepSeek said about 60% of Harness users counted among users of its official model API already run third-party plugins¹⁰.

Those two numbers together are the actual competitive position. Anthropic has larger distribution and a stronger brand. DeepSeek has a more complete open architecture and a formally proven uninstall path. Neither company wins on what the mod is called.

On plugin standardization, which is the thing everyone hopes for: it will not happen soon, and not happening is the better outcome. What the two sides are competing over is not the format, it is control of the runtime. The hook event names and the $ namespace are explicitly Anthropic's, and the docs say the API may change between releases, while Cordis has 350 projects depending on it. If the two actually unified, one of them would be handing over its architectural advantage. Formats converge; semantics do not, because semantics is where the answer to "who owns this agent" lives.

So the next time some agent ships a plugin mechanism, do not ask whether it should be called a mod. Ask three questions. Are extension points tiered with a trust root that fails closed? Is unload a structural guarantee or the author's memory? How many days does it take a plugin author to ship a fix after a breaking core release? Two "no" answers out of three and that plugin system becomes the next Emacs load-theme directory: loud for a quarter, then...

![Cover](assets/x-articles/2102065903517253824-cover.jpg)

Jev is not the next agent route. It is the quiet end of the assumption that the agent is the model.

On September 15, 2026, Diogo Almeida ended two years of stealth and released Jev through TypeSafe AI, alongside a $40 million seed round led by DCVC¹. Almeida co-authored the InstructGPT paper and is one of the people who built RLHF, the method that taught language models to talk to people. 

The model he shipped this time refuses to talk. It generates no text, writes no code, holds no conversation. You hand it a block of state and a set of questions whose answer space you defined in advance, and it returns typed answers with probabilities³. Three primitives only: Choice picks one option from up to 255, Score places the input on an ordered scale, and Noul returns the probability that a yes/no claim is true³. 

TypeSafe calls the category "System One," borrowing Kahneman's fast and intuitive mode. The name comes from Jevons paradox².

![The entire interface: pick one, place on a scale, answer yes or no. No generated string ever leaves the model. Source: langchain.com | Sources [9]](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSwHPRnbkAErd-Y.jpg)

A man who taught AI to speak built a model that won't. That contrast is the best marketing in the launch and the biggest smoke screen in the coverage.

The headline numbers are severe. Seventy to five hundred milliseconds end to end, against 3 to 329 seconds for frontier models⁴. Input at $0.042 per million tokens, output free, because there is no output token³. The homepage banner claims 193.6x faster and 444.6x cheaper, and TypeSafe itself labels those figures as the high end of real-world gains⁴.

![Jev sits at the far cheap end with mid-tier accuracy. Nothing else on the chart is both cheaper and more accurate, which is the actual claim. Source: typesafe.ai | Sources [4]](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSwHvIZaUAAcVpg.png)

On TypeSafe's own four-workflow evaluation, Jev averages 67.8% agreement at $0.0004 and 0.4 seconds per case. GPT-5.6 Sol reaches 74.1% at $0.0836 and 23.3 seconds. Claude Opus 5 reaches 73.1% at $0.1761 and 37.8 seconds⁵. 

Jev is not the most accurate model on its own chart; it is the only point nothing dominates on both axes at once. Broken out, the spread widens: 76.0% on customer service, but 61.8% on invoice processing against Sol's 79.1%, a seventeen-point gap⁶. And the famous "0% hallucination" has to be read exactly. TypeSafe's own wording: "our number is not empirical. Schema matching is guaranteed"⁶. The type can never be wrong. The judgment still can.

![The 0% column is a structural guarantee, not a measurement. On the same chart, Haiku 4.5 breaks structured output 45.5% of the time and Sol fails tool calls 17.0% of the time. Format is a real wound in this industry, and it is a different wound from being wrong. Source: typesafe.ai | Sources [6]](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSwH8-jbcAA1sUU.png)

Type-correct is not judgment-correct.

The most convincing evidence for Jev arrived five days later, from outside TypeSafe, and from a use case nobody was watching. On September 20, LangChain published a controlled test of Jev as a judge over agent traces: five frozen weather-agent runs from LangChain's own open-source harness, each graded 100 times against a human-labeled oracle. 

Jev matched the human on all 500 binary pass/fail decisions. GPT-5.6 Terra hit 99.8%, Luna 96.4%, Claude Sonnet 4.6 80.0%. Jev's per-case quality-score variance was 0.0000149, between 92x and 913x lower than the three language-model judges. It cost $0.00035 per call and $0.34 in total, against $28.17 for Claude⁹.

![The evaluator path most teams actually shipped: an autoregressive model writes a rationale, then code parses that text back into a score. Jev returns the score directly. Source: langchain.com | Sources [9]](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSwIHr9bYAA5DFf.jpg)

Notice what LangChain did not do. They did not let Jev run the agent. They let Jev grade the agent.

That is the part worth keeping.

A product like Jev needs to exist because the last three years of agent engineering made one architectural mistake and then spent enormous effort patching it: we put control flow inside an autoregressive sampling loop. An agent run contains dozens of tiny decisions. Did this step succeed. Call tool A or tool B. Stop or continue. Those are control-flow questions, and we answered them by sampling tokens and parsing the result.

![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSwIZixaMAAxVuX.png)

So a whole layer grew up around the mistake: JSON schema constraints, function-call retries, routers, guardrails, judge calls, and pages of prompt text begging the model to stay in format. That layer is string patching a type system.

Jev's actual move is small and structural. Give the judgment a type, and put the control flow back in the code. Almeida says it flatly in the launch thread: "We believe that the future is code + AI"². That sentence is the thesis. It is not a claim that the model becomes the agent. It is a claim that the model becomes a function the program calls.

Jev is not making agents more agentic. It is demoting the agent from a model to a function.

Which is why "will this be the new agent route" is the wrong question. Model-as-agent and program-as-agent were never parallel tracks, and Jev shoves the whole stack onto the second one. The name is a bet in the same direction. Jevons paradox does not say cheap things get used less; it says cheap things get used far more, in places nobody bothered to use them. Judgment cheap enough to be free will not produce more agents. It dissolves the word "agent" into infrastructure. After SQL, nobody said they wanted to buy a database query robot.

![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSwIyU7a8AA1PeE.png)

The ceiling is as clear as the pitch. Calibration is a population-level property: a 0.83 confidence describes the batch, not this call¹⁰. Compose a dozen Jev calls into one workflow and nothing guarantees the calibration survives your thresholds. The architecture is undisclosed, which ends the conversation in finance, insurance and medicine, where a decision has to be defensible in writing¹⁰. Every's independent test found Jev 25x faster and 580x cheaper than a frontier model, and also found that one of seven planted defects went undetected across three retries⁷. 

A non-peer-reviewed run of 6,560 requests saw a single failure, but semantically identical renamings and reorderings still changed the answers¹¹. Single-shot Jev scored 62.6% on a phishing-link check; splitting the question into five narrow signals and combining them in ordinary code took it to 95.1%, which is the signature of a feature extractor, not a decision maker⁸. And LangChain, the source of the most flattering test so far, supplies the counterweight itself: low cost can amplify mistakes, and a consistently wrong evaluator generates bad feedback at scale⁹. Every published result lands in the same place. Useful as a sentinel. Unsafe as a verdict.

So the likely end state is not a smarter agent, it is a tiered system. A scheduler decides which judgment goes where. A frontier model does the slow thinking. A Jev-class model fires millisecond calls. Deterministic code executes. The scheduler is where the word "agent" actually belongs, and it is the least glamorous part of the stack.

Jev did not open a new agent route. It handed the word "agent" back its coordinates.

Whether it grows into the thing it promises, whether the price holds, when the architecture is published, who is accountable when a 0.91 turns out wrong… all of that is still open. 

One thing is already settled. The moment judgment became cheap enough to insert anywhere, the thing we had been calling an agent turned out to be a handful of decision primitives with a control flow around them.

![Cover](assets/x-articles/2094040899294777617-cover.jpg)

After switching my GenAI developer career from Consumer side to Business side, I have been overdosed by "our company/startup is Palantir in XYZ……“ intro recently.

Most companies blindly copying the Palantir model are not trying to build Palantir. They are trying to rent an AI-company multiple. What they get, in the end, is a high-cost services shop. 

Palantir has been using FDEs as its execution layer for more than a decade. On Wall Street the label was dressed-up Accenture. The 2020 listing produced a pop. By 2022 the stock was lying in the gutter.

![Source: https://www.tikr.com/blog/palantir-stock-has-dropped-31-from-its-peak-heres-where-pltr-could-go-in-2026](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HQ9-LJXagAAyHVg.jpg)

The Forward Deployed Engineer role is not a 2024 invention. Palantir stood it up in the early 2000s, embedding engineers in Afghan bases, Midwestern factories, and classified intelligence shops. Internally they were "Delta," walled off from "Dev," who wrote the platform at HQ.¹ 

Former employee Nabeel Qureshi wrote about spending a year inside Airbus's Toulouse plant, four days a week on the shop floor, helping pull A350 throughput up by 4x.¹ Wall Street still booked the whole machine as outsourcing, consulting, a bodies business, for fourteen years. 

In 2020 the short seller Citron called it a casino and slapped a $20 target on it.² Palantir went public that year, the stock ran, and 2022 smashed it back to the floor. "Lying in the gutter" is not a flourish. It was the actual narrative.²⁴

Here is the part people skip. FDE was already making Palantir money before this GenAI hype cycle. Revenue grew 41% in 2021 and 24% in 2022. Net dollar retention hit 131%, 150% in U.S. commercial, and commercial customer count doubled.⁵ Growth was there. The 2022 stock still fell 64% and broke $6.⁴ 

Why? The texture of the growth failed the test. Years of GAAP losses. A $374 million net loss in 2022. Stock-based compensation once near 30% of revenue. Gross margin stuck around 78%. The market saw a consulting firm with a software skin and paid it like a services vendor.⁵¹¹

FDE is the growth engine. If the engine does not smoke, valuation does not catch.

![Illustration: twenty years of field code, then AIP, GAAP profit, and the multiple. Not a primary source.](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HQ97nLyaMAAVj7N.jpg)

What lit the financials was AIP, shipped in April 2023. Karp said it plainly in the May 2023 shareholder letter: "We began building years ago the foundational architecture" that lets large models create value on private data.⁶ The 2024 annual letter added the punchline: after nearly two decades of investment, they had become "a fundamentally new software business."⁷ 

AIP's job was to productize twenty years of FDE field craft, ontology, and deployment patterns into a platform. Data integration and go-live that used to take months could stand up in hours. They ran 500-plus bootcamps in 2023 alone.⁷ Then the stack: consecutive GAAP profits (2023 was the first profitable year in the company's life), S&P 500 eligibility, passive money, a 167% stock in 2023 and another 340% in 2024.⁴⁷

![PLTR weekly from Finviz. The 2022 floor under $6 and the 2023–24 re-rate are the longer arc in the text; the chart is the live tape, still moving on narrative as much as on FDE headcount. Source: Finviz | sources [2][4]](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HQ97SkwbcAAtVr0.png)

FDE turns knowledge on the customer site into code. AIP turns that code into a platform you can sell. The first pile took twenty years. The second detonated in a few months.

So "the financials finally stood up" is three things stacked: 

1. the asset FDE spent twenty years accumulating

2. AIP as the monetization lever

3. index inclusion as the amplifier

FDE itself did not change. What changed is that Palantir finally proved this pile of expensive humans can grow software gross margin.

Why, in twenty years, is there only one Palantir? a16z partner Marc Andrusko's January piece, "The Palantirization of Everything," is the cleanest cut. He opens with a table. Among top SaaS and AI names, Palantir trades at 76.5x next-twelve-months revenue. Cloudflare is 28.3x. Shopify is 15.6x. This is not "one of the leaders." It is an outlier.³ Andrusko, citing Everest, calls Palantir a "category of one" because it does three things at once: 

1. ships an integrated product platform

2. embeds elite engineers inside customer operations

3. has been proven in life-or-death government work

Most companies can do one of those. Two, if they are lucky. Not three.³

![Among top software/AI companies Palantir trades at 76.5x NTM revenue, versus Cloudflare at 28.3x and Shopify at 15.6x. a16z's visual case for "category of one." Image: a16z (Clouded Judgement / @jaminball) | source [3]](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HQ98a0CagAAE2DG.png)

Inside that stack, FDE is the surface execution layer, not the core. Palantir's actual core is platform-first: data models, permissions, workflow engines, APIs, reusable primitives built before anyone is sent on-site. 

Foundry is the crystallization of hundreds of microservices. The five-piece kit (Gotham, Apollo, Foundry, Ontology, AIP) each owns a different job.³ FDEs in the field assemble and validate those primitives, then feed high-frequency patterns back into the platform. Internally they call it going from gravel road to paved highway.¹³ 

Andrusko's verdict is blunt: copy only the execution layer and you get "Palantir for X," which becomes "Accenture for X" with a nicer frontend.³

![Illustration: platform primitives plus a feedback loop versus renaming pre-sales. Not a primary source.](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HQ99Iasa4AAVsZ3.jpg)

His four failure modes are specific. Sell to mid-market accounts trying to optimize an 8% sales process, and months of embedding cannot clear ROI. Most enterprises do not want to be your forever flagship consulting project. Talent density does not scale when you rename pre-sales to FDE and ask junior generalists to do three jobs. Leadership falls in love with the aesthetic without having watched a real deployment.³ His test for whether the model can copy is more useful than the slogans: 

1. fatality of the problem (counterterror, fraud, battlefield logistics versus an 8% optimization)

2. customer concentration (a few accounts at tens of millions a year)

3. domain isomorphism

4. regulatory / data gravity

You need at least three of the four.³ 

Meanwhile, about 95% of startups blindly hiring FDEs are on an expensive detour. A fully loaded competent FDE runs $220k–$400k a year. Park that person on a $50k ACV account and you have negative margin.¹⁰ 

![Illustration: fatality, concentration, isomorphism, data gravity, and the fully loaded bill. Not a primary source.](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HQ9_5UEakAAKd4O.png)

There is also a validation problem on time. Snowflake, Databricks, OpenAI, and AWS only started standing up FDE-scale teams in 2025–2026. They have not even closed a full fiscal year.⁸ Treating "Palantir got this to work" as "the FDE paradigm is validated" is a category error.

The industry rediscovering FDE, and FDE being proven, are two different facts.

![FDE postings on hiring platforms multiplied in 2025–2026 (a16z citing InterviewQuery, +800–1000%). a16z calls it "the hottest job in tech." What is hot is the title, not a validated model. Image: a16z | source [12]](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HQ-ASGXawAEkZXT.jpg)

Back to the question. Why is this being taken seriously now? 

Two reasons: AI turned the demo-to-production gap into every company's emergency (MIT NANDA's 2025 report: roughly 95% of enterprise GenAI pilots show no measurable P&L impact).⁹ Palantir's 2023–2026 financials proved a labor-heavy path can still grow software margins. 

So the industry rushed to copy the easiest piece: send people on-site. Andrusko's reminder belongs on the wall. Palantir is not "software plus consulting." It is software plus consulting plus a political project plus extremely patient capital.³ That four-piece kit has been run to completion once in twenty years. The only thing between an FDE and staff-aug is a P&L. 

If field code flows back into platform assets, it is a product-discovery engine. If it does not, it is the high-cost services firm in the opening line...
